title: Errands
goal: Get cash and change money, buy medicine, sort out a SIM card or a broken phone, and get clothes, hair and parcels taken care of — saying what needs doing and who does it.
intro:
A normal day in Kabul or Peshawar is full of small errands: the ATM that is out of order again, the money changer (صراف) on the corner, the pharmacy, the phone-repair stall where a smashed screen is fixed in an hour, the tailor who is stitching your clothes for a wedding, the barber, the courier office. People here get things **fixed** rather than replaced, and every errand comes with a little conversation.

In this unit you'll learn the words for these errands and the grammar for **getting things done**: the difference between 'it broke / it got fixed' and 'I broke it / he fixed it', and how Pashto says 'I had my hair cut' or 'I gave my phone in to be repaired'.

grammar.title: 'It broke' vs 'I broke it': کېدل and کول pairs
grammar.body:
Most things that 'happen' in Pashto come in **pairs**: an **intransitive** verb for 'it happens (by itself)' and a **transitive** verb for 'someone does it'. With adjectives the pair is made with **کېدل** 'become' and **کول** 'make':

مات شو 'it broke' · مات کړ 'he broke it'
خراب شو 'it stopped working' · خراب کړ 'he broke it'
جوړ شو 'it got fixed' · جوړ کړ 'he fixed it'
پاک شو 'it got clean' · پاک کړ 'he cleaned it'

Some verbs have the pair built in, with **-edəl** (intransitive) and **-awəl** (transitive): **جوړېدل / جوړول**, **بدلېدل / بدلول**, **ګرمېدل / ګرمول**. Present: ټيلفون جوړېږي 'the phone is being fixed' / مستري ټيلفون جوړوي 'the repairman is fixing the phone'.

**How to choose:** if you don't know or don't care who did it — which is most of the time at a repair shop — use the **کېدل** side: ټيلفون مې مات شو 'my phone broke', کله به جوړ شي؟ 'when will it be fixed?'. If you say who did it, use the **کول** side, and remember that in the past it is **ergative** (unit 16): **ما** ټيلفون مات **کړ** 'I broke the phone', **مستري** ټيلفون جوړ **کړ** 'the repairman fixed the phone'.

The adjective **agrees** like any adjective: ټيلفون خراب شو (m), but نسخه ورک**ه** شوه, ږيره جوړ**ه** شوه (f). The perfective helpers are: کېدل → **شي** (will / should happen), **شو / شوه** (happened); کول → **کړي**, **کړ / کړه / کړل**.

**The trap:** English 'my phone broke' has no doer, so don't use کړ: ټيلفون مې مات **کړ** means 'I broke my phone'.

grammar.title: Getting it done: 'I had my hair cut'
grammar.body:
English has a special pattern for jobs that someone else does for you: 'I **had** my hair cut', 'I'm **getting** my phone fixed'. Pashto usually doesn't bother: it uses the **ordinary verb**, and everyone understands that the barber or the tailor did the work:

ويښتان مې لنډ کړل 'I had my hair cut short' (lit. I made my hair short)
د واده لپاره نوې جامې جوړوم 'I'm having new clothes made for the wedding'

When you need to say **who** does the job, there are three everyday patterns:

1. **X ته ورکول چې + subjunctive** 'give it to X so that he …': ټيلفون مې مستري ته ورکړ **چې** جوړ يې **کړي** 'I gave my phone to the repairman to fix'.
2. **د + infinitive in -o + لپاره** 'for …-ing': جامې مې **د مينځلو لپاره** ورکړې 'I gave my clothes in to be washed'. The infinitive is a noun, so after د it takes the oblique plural ending **-o**: مينځل → مينځلو, اتو → د اتو لپاره.
3. **X ته ووايه چې + subjunctive** 'tell X to …': خياط ته ووايه چې لنډ يې **کړي** 'tell the tailor to shorten it'.

For 'it needs doing', use **بايد** + the intransitive side (grammar 1): دا **بايد بدل شي** 'this needs changing', ويښتان دې بايد لنډ شي 'your hair needs cutting'.

To the professional himself, just use the imperative: **لنډ يې کړه** (informal) / **لنډ يې کړئ** (polite).

lines.native: هو، د صراف څنګ ته. خو هغه هم ډېر ځله خراب وي.
lines.roman: ho, də sarrā́f tsang ta. xo haġá ham ḍer dzə́la xarā́b wi.
lines.en: Yeah, next to the money changer's. But that one's often broken too.

lines.roman: ṣə, tə dálta kéna, zə zhər rā́dzəm.

culture: Errands in the Pashtun region are personal. People have **their** barber, **their** tailor and **their** repairman (مستري), and address them as ورور 'brother', کاکا 'uncle' (to an older man) or by name + جان — not with the formal تاسو and لطفاً of an office. Talking to your barber or the boy at the repair stall with ته and a plain imperative (لنډ يې کړه) is normal; use تاسو with older shopkeepers and the pharmacist. **Cash is still king**: many shops don't take cards, ATMs are often empty or out of order, and in Afghanistan most people change dollars at a صراف — Kabul's huge money market, *Sarai Shahzada*, sets the rate the whole country uses. Men get their shalwar kameez **stitched** rather than bought ready-made, and tailors are swamped in the weeks before Eid and the wedding season, so order early and ask کله به تيار وي؟ — then add a day or two. Phone top-ups are bought as scratch cards in Afghanistan (کارت اچول) and as 'easyload' (ايزي لوډ) in Pakistan.

tip.title: Taking out and putting in: ايستل، اچول
tip.body:
- **ايستل** 'take out' uses the stem **باس-**: پيسې **باسم** 'I'm taking out money', بايد پيسې **وباسم** 'I need to take out money', **وباسه**! 'take it out!'
- **اچول** 'put in': پيسې **اچوم**، **واچوم**، **واچوه**!
- After بايد, غواړم and in commands use the **perfective** (with و-).

lessons.title: My phone broke

tip.title: 'It broke' or 'I broke it'? شو / کړ
tip.body:
- No doer, it just happened: adjective + **شو / شوه** (past), **شي** (will): ټيلفون مې خراب **شو**، کله به جوړ **شي**؟
- Someone did it: adjective + **کړ / کړه / کړل** (past, ergative), **کړي** (will): **ما** ټيلفون مات **کړ**.
- Same with -edəl / -awəl pairs: جوړېږي 'is being fixed' / جوړوي 'fixes'.
tip.pattern: X مات شو (it broke) · ما X مات کړ (I broke it)

tip.title: Getting it done: 'I had it washed'
tip.body:
- Pashto just uses the normal verb: د واده لپاره نوې جامې **جوړوم** 'I'm having new clothes made'.
- To name who does it: **X ته ورکول چې** + subjunctive, or **X ته ووايه چې** + subjunctive.
- 'For …-ing': **د** + infinitive in **-o** + **لپاره**: د مينځلو لپاره.
- 'It needs doing': **بايد** + … **شي**.

lessons.title: The barber and the courier

tip.title: Talking to the barber
tip.body:
- To a barber, tailor or repairman your own age, the plain **ته** imperative is normal and friendly: لنډ يې **کړه**، برابره يې **کړه**.
- Use **کړئ** and لطفاً with an older man, at the pharmacy or at an office counter.
- **مه** + imperfective for 'don't': لنډ يې **مه کوه**.

sentences.native: ږيره لنډه مه کوه، يوازې برابره يې کړه.
sentences.roman: ẓíra lánḍa ma kawa, yawā́ze barābára ye kṛa.
sentences.en: Don't make the beard short, just tidy it up.

sentences.native: نايي ته ووايه چې ويښتان ډېر لنډ نه کړي.
sentences.roman: nāyí ta wə́wāya che weṣtā́n ḍer lanḍ na kṛi.
sentences.en: Tell the barber not to cut your hair too short.
Send my parcel to Kabul.
What's in the parcel?

sentences.native: پارسل په څو ورځو کې رسېږي؟
sentences.roman: pārsál pə tso wradzó ke raséẓi?
sentences.en: How many days does the parcel take to arrive?

sentences.native: پارسل مې لا نه دی رسېدلی.
sentences.roman: pārsál me lā na day rasedə́lay.
sentences.en: My parcel hasn't arrived yet.

sentences.native: د پارسل رسيد دې ساتلی دی؟
sentences.roman: də pārsál rasíd de sātə́lay day?
sentences.en: Have you kept the parcel receipt?
